notes: Turn ids T1 to T59 number the speaker blocks of zoom-saved-transcript.txt in file order. No speaker has two blocks in a row, so each block is one turn.
alsoAccept lists other kinds a careful consultant could reasonably choose; a match on any of them counts.
Nomvula Khumalo is the consultant. Hennie Swanepoel and Charmaine Pillay are the client, and both agreed to the transcript and the local AI at T2 and T3.

Tricky cases: T17's 'about 120 a day' is corrected at T41 (V6 holds the corrected figure); T32 is an assumption to be checked (V14); the deposit at T39 is the consultant's suggestion, not agreed (V18); the VetDesk risk is spread over T47 and T48 (V20); online medical history is explicitly ruled out at T45 (V19); the consent requirement at T37 is the consultant's wording but the client agrees at T38, so it is confirmed (V17).

findings.statement: Each of the three clinics (Centurion, Irene, Olievenhoutbosch) takes bookings by phone on its own landline and writes them in pencil in a paper diary at reception.
VetDesk Pro holds the clinical records, owners' details, vaccination history and billing. Its calendar isn't used: the receptionists rejected it years ago.

Between 08:00 and 10:00 the phones don't stop and the single receptionist per clinic, who also checks people in and takes payments, misses many calls. Erased and overwritten diary entries cause double bookings.
About 20 no-shows a week across the three clinics, each losing a 30-minute slot.
Fewer missed calls, no double bookings and fewer no-shows; the phones are the top priority, because the receptionists are burning out.
findings.note: The consultant summarises at T14 and Hennie confirms and ranks at T15.

findings.statement: About 160 appointments a day across the three clinics on a normal day (corrected from the first estimate of 120: Olievenhoutbosch now has a full Saturday morning and Centurion two vets).
findings.note: T17 said 120; Charmaine corrects it at T41 after checking the diaries, and Hennie confirms at T43. A finding that says 120 is wrong.

findings.statement: Bookings roughly double in February and March: annual vaccinations for Christmas puppies, and the rabies drive in March.
A pet owner books on a website from their phone: chooses the clinic and the reason (vaccination, check-up, sick pet), sees open times and books one, then gets a reminder the day before.
Vaccination-due reminders go out automatically, from the due dates VetDesk holds, with a link to book. This replaces the monthly printed list and phone calls.
Receptionists see their clinic's day, move bookings, and enter phone bookings in the same system, because some older clients will never book online.
Phone bookings stay, but the paper diary goes: all bookings go into the one new diary.
Owners can choose a specific vet, but don't have to.
Can sick animals be booked online, and where is the line with emergencies? Hennie to discuss with the other vets.
Most clients would rather get reminders by WhatsApp than SMS. This is Charmaine's feeling from the front desk; to be checked by asking in the waiting room for a week.
findings.note: Stated as an unverified belief. Recording it as confirmed is a status error.

findings.statement: The practice already pays for an SMS bundle through VetDesk, used for account statements.

Owners' phone numbers are personal information under POPIA: they may be used only for their pet's appointments and reminders, never for marketing, and not given to another company for its own purposes. Consent is currently signed on a paper registration form kept at each clinic.
From day one the system records each owner's consent, owners booking online agree before any message is sent, and the company that sends the messages has a written operator agreement.
findings.note: Worded by the consultant at T37, agreed by Hennie at T38, so confirmed rather than suggested.

findings.statement: The consultant proposed taking a R100 deposit for online Saturday bookings, refunded on arrival, to cut no-shows.
findings.note: The consultant's suggestion. Hennie is unsure and will talk to the partners: not agreed.

findings.statement: Owners will not see their pet's medical history or clinical notes online; the project is bookings and reminders only.
findings.note: Sounds like a requirement when the consultant asks at T44, but is explicitly ruled out at T45. Recording 'owners can view medical history' as a requirement is wrong.

findings.statement: VetDesk has an API, but charges for it per clinic, and it took VetDesk three months to switch it on for another practice: a risk to the timeline. The price and a date are to be asked for in writing.
findings.note: Spread over two client turns: T47 (there is an API) and T48 (the cost and the delay). The consultant names it a risk at T49.

findings.statement: Live by 1 February at the latest, before vaccination season; ideally mid-January, so the receptionists have two weeks before the rush.
R180,000 to build it; running costs (messages and hosting) under R2,500 a month for all three clinics.
The logo green, big buttons (people book with a puppy in the other hand), and a web page rather than an app to download.
Simple, one screen if possible; nothing like VetDesk's forty-field screens.
Ordering and paying for pet food online, perhaps next year.

notFindings.why: The consent check at the start of the meeting is recorded on the consent form, not in the record.
Small talk (the Great Dane in the waiting room).
The consultant's own follow-up (sending a summary) is an action, not a finding about the client.
